title: Topology stress & soft-reserve planning with Orion Ventures
summary: Deep technical session to align on autoscale topology for bursty traffic, soft-reserve pool behavior, KV cache repopulation, quantization tradeoffs for 4-bit/8-bit, and VPC/on-prem constraints for Orion's private deployment. Agreed next steps include benchmarks with prewarmed pools and a security doc handoff.
topics: autoscaling topology, soft-reserve vs hard-reserve, priority queueing models, KV cache warmup and repopulation, batch sizing impact on latency, quantization latency/cost tradeoffs, VPC networking constraints, on-prem GPU eviction considerations, runbook for failover

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-15 16:00 PT | Duration: ~72 minutes | Recording ID: ff-20270315-orion-001
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Redwood SRE), Judy Park (Redwood Solutions); Morgan Liu (Orion Dir Eng), Priya Nair (Orion Platform Eng), Diego Ramos (Orion ML Infra), Claire Zhou (Orion SecOps)

Summary (auto-gen): Quick alignment on autoscale topology and soft-reserve policy. Lots of focus on KV cache repopulation and how batching interacts with quantized kernels. Open Qs around VPC latency to on-prem GPUs and eviction behavior on preemptible clusters.

00:00 Alex (AE): Okay hey everyone thanks for joining on a Friday, uh quick agenda — topology, soft-reserve behavior, kv cache warmup, quant tradeoffs, and then ops/runbook. We have about 70 minutes so we'll go deep where you want.
00:18 Morgan (Orion): Thanks Alex, we really want to understand how Redwood would handle our burst patterns — lots of small chat completions then occasional long-generation jobs. Latency SLOs are p99 < 300ms for small completions, long jobs are okay up to 3s avg but we care about throughput.
00:35 Samir (SE): Got it. Can you share the request size distribution now or later? rough percentiles?
00:40 Priya (Orion): We'll share a CSV but rough numbers: 85% are <=64 tokens, 10% 64-512, 5% >512. Bursts are sudden — onboarding flows that hit 1k qps for 30-90 seconds.
01:02 Lena (SRE): Quick clarifier — when you say 1k qps is that concurrent ops or requests per second to same model version?
01:08 Priya: Same model version, same route, yes.
01:15 Samir: Okay, so we need to ensure pool headroom and warm kernels. We talked about "soft-reserve" earlier — small definition: soft-reserve is not hard pinned GPUs, it's a policy that keeps N% of capacity warm and prewarmed containers ready to spin up without eviction. It trades some cost for reduced cold-starts.
01:38 Diego (ML Infra): Curious — do you prewarm KV caches? like prefix caches for session-based chat? we have sticky sessions and we'd like session-level KV reuse.
01:47 Samir: We have automatic KV cache rehydration for prewarmed pools, but repopulation on soft-reserve scaling is tricky. There are two mitigations: 1) proactive prefix caching — we can snapshot common session prefixes and restore on warmup, 2) incremental warmup using sampled traffic to seed KV.
02:10 Claire (SecOps): From a security perspective we need to know what data is persisted in K V cache and encryption-at-rest details for private. also KMS integration since on-prem will use our HSM.
02:22 Alex: We'll include KMS/HSM notes in the security sheet. Quick point — KV cache contents are ephemeral by default, persisted only for session affinity windows; auditing hooks exist but we can disable persistence.
02:36 Morgan: Great. Let's talk capacity models — hard reserve vs soft reserve. What's your recom for a 1k qps 90s burst?
02:45 Samir: If you have predictable bursts, a hybrid approach is ideal. Keep ~20% soft-reserve prewarmed for low-cost warm instances and use burst queues for the rest. We run queueing models internally — typically M/M/c won't match LLM tail behavior, so we use a G/G/c style simulator with heavy-tailed service time. For 1k qps bursts with 64-token median, a 20% soft-reserve reduces p99 tail by ~35% in our sims (rough numbers).
03:25 Priya: The sim numbers sound good, but what's the cost delta?
03:30 Lena: Soft-reserve cost is mostly idle GPU tax and slightly higher memory usage due to KV snapshots. For 20% on a fleet of 10 nodes it's about 18-22% uplift in reserved cost but reduces emergency burst scaling which is expensive.
03:50 Diego: About quantization — would 4-bit quant help tail latency during bursts? we saw mixed results locally.
03:55 Samir: Quant helps throughput and cost, but for tail latency it depends. 4-bit kernels are faster per-token on supported hardware but can increase per-request variance if kernels cause more memory spills on certain seq lengths. Our recommendation: keep 8-bit for latency-sensitive small completions; use 4-bit for background high-throughput paths. We can do mixed-routing: route small high-priority traffic to 8-bit low-latency pool and bulk to 4-bit.
04:30 Morgan: Mixed routing sounds promising. How does that interact with KV cache?
04:35 Samir: KV caches are model-variant specific. If you switch quantization variants you lose kv affinity unless the variants share compatible KV layout. We support KV translation in the runtime but it's costly. Best practice: pin session flows to a variant group.
04:55 Priya: So for our chat use-case we should route the 85% small completions to an 8-bit prewarm soft-reserve pool and bulk jobs into quantized pools?
05:05 Samir: Yes exactly. Also consider small warm pools with continuous batching; continuous batching increases throughput but slightly increases tail for single-request latency, so tune the batch timeout aggressively for p99 targets.
05:28 Claire: On VPC and private deployment: our corporate policy forces egress via on-prem gateways, and we plan to run the inference workers on our colocation GPUs. How does Redwood handle networking overhead?
05:40 Judy (Solutions): We typically run a control plane in Redwood-hosted region and allow a private control plane option for enterprise. For on-prem inference workers, we use a connector via secure tunnel and optional VPC peering. Network egress increases RTT; we do region-aware routing to minimize hops. We'll run a latency probe with your gateway to measure RTTs.
06:02 Morgan: If RTT to on-prem is 25-40ms, that eats into our 300ms p99. How do we compensate?
06:10 Samir: Move latency-sensitive paths entirely on-prem (private control plane or private deployment) so request-to-token generation is local. Use control-plane-in-cloud only for management. That avoids cross-cloud hops. If that's not possible, use edge prefilters to reduce tokens sent for small completions.
06:32 Diego: Back to queueing — you mentioned priority queues and admission control. Could you sketch a simple policy?
06:37 Samir: Sure: two-class priority queue. Class A: small interactive completions (p99 target 300ms) — admission uses prewarmed pool and short batch timeouts (2-5ms), higher CPU/GPU share. Class B: long jobs — queued with relaxed batch timeouts (20-50ms) and routed to quantized pools. When backlog grows, we apply graceful degradation: drop lower-priority batching windows first and shed heavy jobs to background cluster. We also use soft preemption: background jobs can be paused to free KV slots.
07:12 Priya: What's preemption cost? do we lose KV state?
07:15 Samir: Pausing jobs preserves state in memory if the worker stays alive; if worker is evicted we persist session snapshot to disk for short windows. There's a tradeoff: too much preemption increases cold-cache recovery time.
07:30 Morgan: What's cold-start delta for a new worker without KV snapshot vs prewarmed?
07:33 Samir: Cold start (full kernel + model load) on GPU can be 3-12s depending on model size. Warm start with prewarmed container but empty KV is ~150-350ms for small completions; with KV snapshot restore it's 300-700ms depending on KV.
07:55 Lena: Those numbers match our expectations. That 300-700ms can exceed p99 if network RTT is high, so we need to minimize snapshot restores.
08:10 Diego: Can we use lightweight ephemeral KV caching at load balancer level? like route sticky sessions to the same warm worker pool?
08:17 Samir: Yes sticky session affinity is supported; it's one of the simplest ways to keep KV hot. Downside is uneven load distribution in bursts. We recommend a hybrid: soft session affinity with fallback to best-effort routing.
08:34 Priya: For benching, what should we measure? kernels, batch sizes, p50/p95/p99/p999 and cost per token? any other?
08:42 Samir: Also measure KV repopulation time, cold-start rate, and failure modes (eviction latency). Instrument token-level breakdown and tail latency per sequence length bucket. We'll provide a benchmark template.
09:00 Morgan: About prewarmed pool sizing — you suggested 20% — how sensitive is p99 to that percent?
09:07 Samir: In our sims, going from 10% to 20% soft-reserve often halves the cold-start contributions to p99; beyond 30% returns diminish. But depends on burst duration and traffic variance. We'll run sim with your real traces.
09:28 Judy: Any constraints on GPU types for quantized ops? we mostly have A100s and some older V100s on-prem.
09:35 Samir: 4-bit optimized kernels are best on A100/NVIDIA Ampere+ with supported tensor cores. V100 may not see the same speedups and could have memory format mismatches. We'll detect hardware and pick kernel path; in mixed hardware fleets we recommend homogeneous pools for predictable latency.
09:58 Priya: Suppose we can't uniform hardware — what then?
10:02 Samir: Use hardware-aware routing: send latency-sensitive traffic to A100 pool and background to mixed or older GPUs. That increases complexity but keeps SLOs.
10:17 Morgan: Let's talk failover drills — if a whole zone goes down, how does Redwood handle capacity migration?
10:24 Lena: We support multi-region pools and can failover traffic via smart routing. For on-prem hybrid setups, we usually pre-provision fallback hosted capacity to absorb critical traffic. We'll set warm standby pools in a nearby region as a last resort.
10:42 Claire: For audits we need procedure docs — how does Redwood log evictions, KV restores, and model rollbacks?
10:48 Judy: We have audit logs per-request, model versioning events, and eviction traces. We can produce a sample log package.
10:58 Morgan: Good. A couple practical Qs: 1) If we enable soft-reserve 20% and have 1k qps bursts, what's expected cost bump? 2) How long to run a meaningful bench?
11:08 Lena: Cost bump estimated at 18-25% for reserved spend depending on fleet utilization. Bench 2-4 hours with synthetic bursts plus a 24-hour pass to see diurnal effects. But initial bench can run in 2 hours.
11:26 Samir: Also test a mixed quant routing scenario. We'll provide harness that can replay your traces with routing rules.
11:33 Priya: Nice. A quick aside on telemetry: do you expose token-level traces and per-route token cost?
11:38 Judy: Yes — in Redwood Console you get token-level cost, latency breakdown per model and route, and rollout diffs. We can add custom tags for Orion's routes.
11:48 Morgan: Perfect. Any gotchas with KMS/HSM? Claire?
11:52 Claire: We require HSM-backed keys for any persisted session snapshots. Need documented integration and proof-of-concept.
11:58 Alex: We'll include HSM KMS integration steps in the security packet and propose a POC flow.
12:05 Priya: Last topic — throttling strategy during long sustained overload. Do you prefer shed or queue?
12:11 Samir: Graceful shedding: protect priority small completions by throttling background long jobs first. Use admission control to deny or delay new background jobs and return informative 429 with retry-after for clients. Also provide soft quotas per-customer route.
12:28 Morgan: Makes sense. Okay let's recap next steps.
12:31 Alex: Recap: Redwood to run 3 bench variants (Samir), Orion to share trace CSVs and SLAs (Priya), Alex to send security docs, and schedule bench session for week of 2027-03-22. Any final Qs?
12:45 Priya: None from me. Thanks.
12:47 Morgan: Thanks everyone, this was super helpful.
12:50 Meeting end.
